elements.name: Thread Pool
elements.what: A fixed or bounded set of pre-created worker threads that repeatedly take tasks from a queue and execute them, amortizing thread creation cost.
elements.problem: Creating a thread per task wastes creation/teardown cost and allows unbounded resource consumption under load; a pool bounds concurrency and reuses threads.
elements.named_in: Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes, Lea (2006)

elements.name: Executor
elements.what: An abstraction that decouples task submission from the policy of task execution (which thread, when, in what order), typically backed by a work queue and thread pool.
elements.problem: Hard-coding 'new thread per task' couples application logic to an execution policy; an executor lets throughput, ordering, and resource policy vary independently of submitted work.
elements.named_in: Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes, Lea (2006)

elements.name: Future / Promise
elements.what: A placeholder object representing the eventual result of an asynchronous computation, which consumers can query, wait on, or attach continuations to.
elements.problem: A caller wants to start an asynchronous operation and continue working without blocking, yet still obtain the result (or its failure) later in a first-class, composable way.
elements.named_in: Promises: Linguistic Support for Efficient Asynchronous Procedure Calls - Liskov, Shrira (1988)

elements.name: Async-Await Model
elements.what: A language-level model in which functions marked async are compiled into continuation/state-machine form so that awaiting an asynchronous result suspends the function without blocking its thread.
elements.problem: Callback-based asynchronous code inverts control flow and destroys readability; async-await preserves sequential-looking code while keeping execution non-blocking.
elements.named_in: The F# Asynchronous Programming Model - Syme, Petricek, Lomov (2011)

elements.name: Coroutine
elements.what: A routine that can suspend its own execution at yield points and later be resumed with its local state intact, enabling cooperative multitasking on one thread.
elements.problem: Some computations (pipelines, state machines, async I/O) are naturally expressed as multiple interleaved control flows without the cost and preemption hazards of OS threads.
elements.named_in: Design of a Separable Transition-Diagram Compiler - Conway (1963)

elements.name: Green Threads
elements.what: Threads scheduled by a runtime or library in user space rather than by the operating system, multiplexed onto a smaller number of kernel threads.
elements.problem: Kernel threads are expensive to create and context-switch; user-level scheduling permits very large numbers of cheap concurrent activities at the cost of runtime-managed blocking.
elements.named_in: Green thread - Wikipedia

elements.name: Event Loop
elements.what: A single loop that waits for events (I/O readiness, messages, timers) and dispatches each to its handler, serializing all handler execution on one thread.
elements.problem: Handling many concurrent event sources with one thread avoids locking and thread overhead, provided handlers never block the loop; the pattern form for demultiplexing is POSA2's Reactor.
elements.named_in: Event loop - Wikipedia

elements.name: Producer-Consumer
elements.what: One or more producer threads place work items into a shared (usually bounded, blocking) queue from which one or more consumer threads remove and process them.
elements.problem: Producers and consumers run at different, varying rates; a shared buffer decouples them in time, smooths bursts, and bounds memory while coordinating handoff safely.
elements.named_in: Cooperating Sequential Processes - Dijkstra (1965)

elements.name: Work Stealing
elements.what: Each worker keeps its own deque of tasks and, when idle, steals tasks from the tail of other workers' deques, balancing load with minimal contention.
elements.problem: A single shared task queue becomes a contention bottleneck and balances load poorly for fine-grained, dynamically spawned tasks; per-worker deques with stealing keep processors busy cheaply.
elements.named_in: Scheduling Multithreaded Computations by Work Stealing - Blumofe, Leiserson (1999)

elements.name: Fork-Join
elements.what: A task forks subtasks that run in parallel and then joins on their completion, typically applied recursively to divide-and-conquer problems.
elements.problem: Recursive decomposable work needs a structured way to express parallelism whose task graph mirrors the call tree, keeping synchronization implicit in the join points.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Parallel Programming - Mattson, Sanders, Massingill (2004)

elements.name: Thread Confinement
elements.what: Restricting all access to mutable data to a single thread, making synchronization unnecessary for that data.
elements.problem: Shared mutable state requires locking that is easy to get wrong; if data is only ever touched by one thread (e.g., a UI thread or per-connection handler), thread safety follows by construction.
elements.named_in: Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes, Lea (2006)

elements.name: Thread-Local Storage
elements.what: A mechanism giving each thread its own independent copy of a logically global variable, accessed through one name but resolved per thread.
elements.problem: Code needs per-thread context (allocators, errno, transaction context) without threading it through every call signature and without contended shared state.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Safe Publication
elements.what: The set of idioms (final fields, volatile references, locks, initialized statics, concurrent collections) that make an object and its state visible to other threads in a fully constructed form.
elements.problem: Handing a reference from a constructing thread to another thread without a happens-before edge can expose partially constructed state; publication must use a memory-model-sanctioned channel.
elements.named_in: Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes, Lea (2006)
elements.borderline: More a memory-model correctness discipline than a standalone mechanism, but it is named, recurring, and taught as a unit in JCiP; charter flags it borderline and includes it.

elements.name: Immutable Object
elements.what: An object whose observable state cannot change after construction, making it freely shareable across threads without synchronization.
elements.problem: Mutable shared state is the root cause of most concurrency errors; objects that never change need no locks, no defensive copies, and no visibility protocol beyond safe publication.
elements.named_in: Patterns in Java, Volume 1: A Catalog of Reusable Design Patterns Illustrated with UML - Grand (1998)

elements.name: Copy-on-Write
elements.what: Sharing a single underlying representation among readers and copying it only at the moment of modification, so readers never need locks and writers pay the copy cost.
elements.problem: Read-mostly shared data suffers under locking; replacing the whole structure atomically on each (rare) write gives readers an always-consistent snapshot with zero coordination.
elements.named_in: Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes, Lea (2006)

elements.name: Monitor
elements.what: A construct bundling shared data, the procedures that operate on it, and mutual exclusion so that at most one thread executes inside the monitor at a time, with condition variables for waiting.
elements.problem: Scattering lock acquire/release across client code invites races and deadlocks; encapsulating exclusion with the data it protects centralizes the synchronization policy.
elements.named_in: Monitors: An Operating System Structuring Concept - Hoare (1974)

elements.name: Condition Variable
elements.what: A queue on which threads wait, releasing an associated lock, until another thread signals that a state predicate may now hold; woken threads re-acquire the lock and re-test the predicate.
elements.problem: Threads must wait efficiently for a condition over shared state to become true; busy-polling wastes CPU and naive sleep/wake without a lock protocol loses wakeups.
elements.named_in: Monitors: An Operating System Structuring Concept - Hoare (1974)

elements.name: Semaphore
elements.what: An integer counter with atomic wait (decrement-or-block) and signal (increment-and-wake) operations, used to control access to a pool of permits.
elements.problem: Programs need to bound how many threads enter a region or consume a finite resource, and to signal occurrence of events between threads, with primitive-level generality.
elements.named_in: Cooperating Sequential Processes - Dijkstra (1965)

elements.name: Mutex
elements.what: A lock providing mutual exclusion: at most one thread holds it at a time, serializing execution of the critical sections it guards.
elements.problem: Concurrent reads and writes to shared mutable state produce race conditions; a mutex establishes exclusive ownership for the duration of each compound action.
elements.named_in: Solution of a Problem in Concurrent Programming Control - Dijkstra (1965)

elements.name: Reentrant Lock
elements.what: A mutex variant that the holding thread may re-acquire without deadlocking, tracked by owner and hold count; charter-noted as a variant of the plain mutex kept separate for its distinct semantics.
elements.problem: Lock-guarded methods that call other guarded methods on the same object self-deadlock under a non-reentrant mutex; reentrancy makes lock acquisition composable within one thread.
elements.named_in: Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes, Lea (2006)

elements.name: Readers-Writer Lock
elements.what: A lock admitting either many concurrent readers or one exclusive writer, exploiting the fact that reads do not conflict with each other.
elements.problem: Read-mostly data serialized behind a plain mutex forfeits read parallelism; distinguishing shared from exclusive access recovers it at the cost of fairness/starvation policy decisions.
elements.named_in: Concurrent Control with 'Readers' and 'Writers' - Courtois, Heymans, Parnas (1971)

elements.name: Spinlock
elements.what: A lock acquired by busy-waiting (repeatedly testing an atomic flag) instead of blocking, trading CPU cycles for elimination of scheduler round-trips.
elements.problem: For very short critical sections, or contexts where blocking is impossible (interrupt handlers, kernels), the cost of putting a thread to sleep exceeds the cost of spinning.
elements.named_in: The Performance of Spin Lock Alternatives for Shared-Memory Multiprocessors - Anderson (1990)

elements.name: Latch
elements.what: A one-shot synchronizer that blocks waiting threads until it reaches its terminal (open) state - typically when a count of prerequisite events reaches zero - and then stays open forever.
elements.problem: Threads must not proceed until some set of initialization steps or prerequisite tasks has completed exactly once; a latch expresses this irreversible ready condition directly.
elements.named_in: Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes, Lea (2006)

elements.name: Barrier
elements.what: A synchronization point at which each thread in a group waits until all members arrive, after which all are released together; cyclic barriers reset for reuse across iterations.
elements.problem: Phased parallel computations (e.g., iterative stencil or simulation steps) require that no thread start phase N+1 while others are still in phase N.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Parallel Programming - Mattson, Sanders, Massingill (2004)

elements.name: Guarded Suspension
elements.what: A method that suspends the calling thread until a precondition (guard) over the object's state becomes true, then executes; the wait-loop-on-condition-variable pattern form.
elements.problem: An operation only makes sense in certain object states; rather than failing or polling, the caller blocks until another thread changes the state and signals.
elements.named_in: Patterns in Java, Volume 1: A Catalog of Reusable Design Patterns Illustrated with UML - Grand (1998)

elements.name: Balking
elements.what: A method that immediately returns (or reports failure) instead of waiting when the object is not in an appropriate state to execute the request.
elements.problem: Some requests are only valid in a particular state and are pointless to queue (e.g., saving when no changes are dirty, starting an already-started service); refusing beats blocking.
elements.named_in: Patterns in Java, Volume 1: A Catalog of Reusable Design Patterns Illustrated with UML - Grand (1998)

elements.name: Two-Phase Termination
elements.what: Shutting down a thread or active object by setting a termination request flag (phase 1) that the target observes at safe points, then letting it release resources and exit cleanly (phase 2).
elements.problem: Forcibly killing threads corrupts shared state and leaks resources; termination must be a cooperative protocol in which the thread finishes or abandons work at well-defined points.
elements.named_in: Patterns in Java, Volume 1: A Catalog of Reusable Design Patterns Illustrated with UML - Grand (1998)

elements.name: Scheduler
elements.what: An object that explicitly sequences waiting threads' access to a resource according to a scheduling policy (FIFO, priority, deadline) instead of leaving the order to the lock implementation.
elements.problem: When the order in which contending threads proceed matters (fairness, priorities, deadlines), the policy must be lifted out of the lock and made an explicit, pluggable decision.
elements.named_in: Patterns in Java, Volume 1: A Catalog of Reusable Design Patterns Illustrated with UML - Grand (1998)

elements.name: Pipeline Parallelism
elements.what: Decomposing a computation into ordered stages, each run by its own thread(s) and connected by queues, so different data items are processed in different stages simultaneously.
elements.problem: A sequential multi-stage transformation of a data stream leaves all but one stage idle; overlapping stages on different items converts stage count into throughput.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Parallel Programming - Mattson, Sanders, Massingill (2004)

elements.name: Actor Model
elements.what: Concurrency organized as isolated actors that share no state and interact only by asynchronous messages to mailboxes, each actor processing one message at a time and able to create actors and change behavior.
elements.problem: Shared-state locking scales and composes poorly; giving each concurrent entity private state and a serialized mailbox eliminates data races by construction.
elements.named_in: A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence - Hewitt, Bishop, Steiger (1973)
elements.borderline: In-process actor frameworks (Akka on one JVM, Erlang processes in one node, actor libraries in C++/Rust) pass the altitude test; distributed actor systems as deployment topology are architecture-level and belong to Phase 3.

elements.name: CSP Channel
elements.what: A typed conduit through which concurrent processes communicate and synchronize by sending and receiving values, with rendezvous (unbuffered) or bounded-buffer semantics.
elements.problem: Threads need to exchange data and coordinate without exposing shared mutable state; making communication the synchronization ('share memory by communicating') removes explicit locking.
elements.named_in: Communicating Sequential Processes - Hoare (1978)

elements.name: Lock Striping
elements.what: Partitioning a data structure's protection across an array of locks (e.g., one per hash-bucket group) so independent operations contend only on their stripe.
elements.problem: A single lock over a large structure serializes logically independent operations; striping trades a bounded increase in lock count for near-linear reduction in contention.
elements.named_in: Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes, Lea (2006)

elements.name: Double-Checked Locking
elements.what: Lazy initialization that tests the initialized flag once without the lock, and only on a miss acquires the lock and tests again before initializing; requires memory-model support (volatile/atomics) to be correct.
elements.problem: Guarding every access to a lazily initialized singleton with a lock costs a lock round-trip on the hot path; the double check pays synchronization only until initialization completes. Famously broken without proper fences - the naming literature documents both the pattern and its hazard.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Master/Worker
elements.what: A master decomposes a job into independent tasks placed in a shared bag/queue; a set of workers repeatedly grab and execute tasks until the bag is empty, giving automatic load balance.
elements.problem: Tasks of unpredictable and uneven size defeat static assignment to processors; dynamic self-scheduling from a shared task pool balances load without global analysis.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Parallel Programming - Mattson, Sanders, Massingill (2004)

elements.name: SPMD
elements.what: All processing elements run the same program, using their unique id to select the data partition and branch to role-specific behavior.
elements.problem: Writing and deploying one distinct program per processor does not scale; a single parameterized program keeps parallel code maintainable while allowing per-rank specialization.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Parallel Programming - Mattson, Sanders, Massingill (2004)

elements.name: Loop Parallelism
elements.what: Distributing the iterations of a (semantically independent) loop across threads, typically via compiler directives or a parallel-for library construct.
elements.problem: Much compute time in existing sequential programs concentrates in loops; parallelizing iterations in place yields speedup with minimal restructuring when iterations are independent.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Parallel Programming - Mattson, Sanders, Massingill (2004)

elements.name: Rendezvous
elements.what: A synchronization in which two tasks must both arrive at a meeting point (a call and a matching accept) before either proceeds, with data optionally exchanged during the meeting.
elements.problem: Direct task-to-task interaction sometimes requires both parties present simultaneously - combining synchronization and communication in one atomic step rather than via shared buffers.
elements.named_in: Reference Manual for the Ada Programming Language - ANSI/MIL-STD-1815A (1983)

elements.name: Read-Copy-Update
elements.what: Readers traverse shared data with essentially zero synchronization while updaters publish new versions atomically and defer reclamation of old versions until all pre-existing readers have finished (a grace period).
elements.problem: Read-mostly kernel/data-plane structures cannot afford reader-side locks or atomics; RCU shifts the entire coordination cost to the rare update path.
elements.named_in: Read-Copy Update: Using Execution History to Solve Concurrency Problems - McKenney, Slingwine (1998)

elements.name: Software Transactional Memory
elements.what: Shared-memory operations grouped into transactions that execute optimistically and commit atomically, aborting and retrying on conflict, giving composable lock-free-style synchronization.
elements.problem: Locks do not compose - correct lock-based components combine into deadlock-prone systems; transactions let programmers state atomicity declaratively and leave conflict resolution to the runtime.
elements.named_in: Software Transactional Memory - Shavit, Touitou (1995)

elements.name: Compare-and-Swap Loop
elements.what: The nonblocking update idiom: read the current value, compute a new value, and atomically install it only if the location still holds the value read, retrying on failure.
elements.problem: Lock-based updates of single words suffer contention, priority inversion, and deadlock risk; a CAS retry loop achieves lock-free progress for small state transitions.
elements.named_in: Wait-Free Synchronization - Herlihy (1991)
elements.borderline: The bare CAS instruction is a hardware/ISA primitive below the design band; included for the CAS-retry-loop / atomic-variable design idiom as taught in JCiP ch. 15 and the nonblocking literature.

parked_architecture.name: SEDA (Staged Event-Driven Architecture)
parked_architecture.why: Welsh et al. 2001 - a whole-service structure of event-driven stages connected by queues with per-stage admission control; primarily a statement of system-level structure (charter directs it here).

parked_architecture.name: Half-Sync/Half-Async
parked_architecture.why: POSA2 labels it an architectural pattern: it layers an entire concurrent system into synchronous and asynchronous service layers with a queueing layer between - system structuring, not an in-component mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: MapReduce
parked_architecture.why: Dean & Ghemawat 2004 - a cluster-scale programming model plus execution framework/topology; the in-program kernel of it is covered by master/worker + pipeline elements.

excluded_notable.name: Memory barrier / fence
excluded_notable.why: Hardware/ISA-level ordering instruction below the design band (raw instruction granularity, like a keyword); its design-level surface appears inside safe publication, DCL, and CAS entries.

excluded_notable.name: LMAX Disruptor
excluded_notable.why: A specific product/library, not a named recurring element; its mechanisms fold into ring buffer (data-flow scout territory) and single-writer principle.

excluded_notable.name: Bulk Synchronous Parallel (BSP)
excluded_notable.why: Valiant 1990 - an abstract bridging/cost model of parallel computation, not an implementable in-program mechanism; its in-program echo is the barrier element.

excluded_notable.name: Initialization-on-demand holder idiom
excluded_notable.why: Java-specific micro-idiom (class-loader-based lazy init); a language-level alternative realization of what double-checked locking covers - variant-level, folded into DCL's territory.

excluded_notable.name: Nuclear reaction pattern
excluded_notable.why: Listed on Wikipedia's concurrency-pattern page but with no established catalog/textbook naming source found; fails the establishedness gate rather than the altitude test.

notes: Charter list fully covered (33/33 charter elements including borderline safe-publication and POSA-owned DCL) plus 7 canon additions from the same sources (Mattson supporting structures: master/worker, SPMD, loop parallelism; plus rendezvous, RCU, STM, CAS loop). Spot-checks this session: Wikipedia concurrency-pattern list (confirms balking, barrier, DCL, guarded suspension, monitor, RW lock, scheduler, thread pool, TLS at title level) and Mattson supporting-structures list (SPMD, Master/Worker, Loop Parallelism, Fork/Join). Deliberately left to sibling scouts: POSA2 event/concurrency patterns other than DCL/TSS (Active Object, Monitor Object as pattern form, Reactor, Proactor, Leader/Followers - assumed POSA scout territory); message queue/mailbox (communication scout); ring/circular and double buffering (data-flow scout); lock-free data structures and hazard pointers (data-structures territory per mission scope rule); priority inheritance/priority ceiling (real-time/embedded scout); optimistic concurrency control (database/persistence scout). Thin spots if no other scout owns them: OS-level primitives (futex, eventfd), select/poll-style demultiplexing as a bare mechanism, structured concurrency (nursery/scope - named in Trio docs and JEP 453, arguably now canon), and Lea's finer-grained vocabulary (fully synchronized object, splitting synchronization).
